text_blocks.snippet: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, making the right side of the heart work too hard.
snippet_highlighted_words: high blood pressure in the lung arteries, making the right side of the heart work too hard

text_blocks.snippet: In the early stages, PAH often causes no symptoms at all. As the condition progresses, signs and symptoms appear—frequently mimicking other heart or lung diseases.

list.snippet: Shortness of breath (dyspnea): Usually starts during exercise or routine tasks (like walking or climbing stairs) and can eventually occur at rest.
Fatigue and weakness: A deep lack of energy or heavy feeling in the body.
Chest pain or pressure: Caused by an overworked and strained right heart muscle.
Dizziness or lightheadedness: Often triggered by exertion or changes in position.
Fainting spells (syncope): Occurs when the brain temporarily receives less oxygen.
Heart palpitations: A fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat.

text_blocks.snippet: As fluid builds up or the heart's right side begins to fail, later-stage signs may develop:

list.snippet: Swelling (edema): Fluid retention in the feet, ankles, legs, or abdomen (ascites).
Cyanosis: A bluish tint to the lips, fingers, or skin due to low blood oxygen levels.
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis): Rare, but can happen as pressure in the lung vessels increases.
Hoarseness: Can occur if an enlarged pulmonary artery presses on nearby chest nerves.

text_blocks.snippet: You can learn more about warning signs and diagnostic pathways through the American Lung Association Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Guide.

list.snippet: Who is experiencing the symptoms (age or general health background)
